extracted.intended_audience: general public and stakeholders (plant breeders, IP students, lawyers, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of statutory eligibility, substantive requirements, rights, exemptions, and related-IP comparisons for plant variety protection under the U.S. Plant Variety Protection Act (PVPA) of 1970.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible reproductive modes
rubrics_metrics.description: The PVPA confers a limited period of legal control to breeders of sexually reproduced or tuber-propagated plant varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes PVPA protection from plant patents (which cover asexually reproduced plants and exclude tuber-propagated plants). The same plant may be eligible under multiple regimes (PVPA, plant patent, utility patent) depending on reproductive mode and patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: New (novelty) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be new: propagating or harvested material has not been sold or otherwise disposed of for purposes of exploitation for more than one year in the United States, or more than four years in any foreign jurisdiction (or six years in the case of a tree or vine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sales/disposal time limits determine statutory novelty. The article summarizes the statutory time-bars that limit eligibility based on prior commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be distinct — clearly distinguishable from any other publicly known variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctness may be based on one or more identifiable morphological, physiological, or other characteristics, including commercially valuable characteristics (example: milling and baking qualities for wheat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be uniform, in the sense that any variations are describable, predictable, and commercially acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity criterion expects within-variety variation to be characterizable and acceptable for commercial use; variations should not undermine the variety's identity or reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The variety must be stable, meaning when reproduced it will remain unchanged with regard to its essential and distinctive characteristics within a reasonable degree of commercial reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability requires that key traits persist through reproduction/repropagation cycles to a commercially reliable degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exclusive rights (what certificate excludes others from doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant variety certificate gives the breeder the right to exclude others from selling the variety, offering it for sale, reproducing it, importing it, exporting it, or using it in producing (as distinguished from developing) a hybrid or different variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerates the core prohibited acts for third parties during the certificate term; note the distinction that 'producing' hybrids using the variety is covered but 'developing' (i.e., breeding) may be treated differently (see research exemption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Term of protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of protection runs 20 years from the certificate's date of issue, or 25 years in the case of a tree or vine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductory text also summarizes that breeders may receive 'up to 25 years' of exclusive control for eligible varieties; the statute provides the specific 20/25-year terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-interest/compulsory-licensing exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: USDA may declare an otherwise protected variety open (compulsory license) on the basis of equitable remuneration if it finds that no more than two years of compulsory licensing is necessary to ensure adequate supply of fiber, food, or feed and that the owner is unwilling or unable to meet public demand at a price reasonably deemed fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exemption limits exclusivity in emergencies or public-need situations; it requires USDA findings and provides for equitable remuneration rather than forfeiture of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The use and reproduction of a protected variety for plant breeding or other bona fide research shall not constitute infringement under the PVPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This carve-out allows breeders and researchers to use protected varieties as inputs for breeding or research without infringing the certificate-holder's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farmer seed-saving exemption (and sale limitation history)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PVPA permits a farmer to save seed from protected varieties and to use such saved seed in the production of a crop without infringement. Prior to 1994 this exemption also allowed farmers to sell such saved seed to others; 1994 amendments eliminated the sales exemption while continuing on-farm saving and replanting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court litigation (Asgrow Seed Co. v. Winterboer) and statutory amendments have defined the current scope: saving and replanting on the farmer's own farm is permitted, but commercial sale of saved seed is no longer an exemption under the amended statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap with plant patents and utility patents / patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant may be eligible for protection under the Patent Act (utility patent) as long as patentability requirements are met; the same plant may be protected by a utility patent as well as a plant variety protection certificate and/or a plant patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court decisions (Diamond v. Chakrabarty and J.E.M. Ag Supply v. Pioneer Hi-Bred) confirmed the availability of utility patents for plants and that sexually reproduced plants eligible for PVPA protection can also be patented, subject to patent criteria (novelty, non-obviousness, utility, written description, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: PVPA's international compliance context
rubrics_metrics.description: The PVPA represents the United States' effort to comply with UPOV (International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants) and TRIPs (the WTO's Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This situates the PVPA within international plant-breeders'-rights norms and trade-related IP commitments; compliance influenced statutory amendments (e.g., 1994 changes).
